draft.title: Choosing a measure of spread
card: It uses every value and is measured around the mean. It suits data that is roughly symmetric with no outliers.
The interquartile range (IQR) is Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle half of the values. Extreme values do not change it much.
Skewed data has a long tail on one side. Data with outliers has a few extreme values. For both, the IQR is the better measure of spread.
Example: house prices in a suburb, with one mansion far above the rest, are skewed. The IQR describes the spread of typical prices better than the standard deviation.
draft.remember: Symmetric with no outliers: standard deviation. Skewed or with outliers: IQR.

a.q: Which data set is best described using the standard deviation as its measure of spread?
opts: Heights of Year 10 students, roughly symmetric
Salaries at a firm, with one boss paid far more
Waiting times, with a long tail of very long waits
Test scores, with two students scoring zero by mistake
a.why: Symmetric data with no outliers suits standard deviation. The other three are skewed or have outliers, so the IQR describes them better.
a.clue: Look for the data with no tail and no extreme values.

b.q: Leila records the daily number of visitors to her market stall in Ballarat. Most days are between 40 and 60, but one festival day had 400. Which measure of spread should she use, and why?
opts: IQR, because the festival day is an outlier
Standard deviation, because it uses every value
Standard deviation, because the data is symmetric
IQR, because it uses every value in the data
b.why: The festival day is an outlier, and the IQR is not changed much by extreme values. Standard deviation is tempting because it uses every value, but that is why one outlier distorts it.
b.clue: Think about which measure one extreme day would distort.
